posts.character: Childhood rules and rituals (holding the TV antenna)
posts.quote: I WAS THE REMOTE CONTROL, AND ON GAME DAY I WAS ALSO THE ANTENNA.
posts.caption: Sunday afternoon, the game was on, and the picture looked like it was snowing inside the set. Dad sent you over to fix the rabbit ears. You'd bend one, twist the other, and wrap a little more tinfoil around the tips while he hollered from his chair: warmer, no, back, right there, don't move. And that was it, you were part of the television now, standing with one arm in the air for the whole fourth quarter. Nobody ever told you who won. You were facing the wall.
posts.first:
My brother and I used to take turns, one quarter each, and we argued about whose quarter had more commercials. Dad swore the reception was better when you stood on one foot. I believed that until I was about twelve.

posts.quote: MONDAY WAS WASH DAY, AND EVERY BACKYARD ON THE BLOCK HAD SHEETS FLAPPING LIKE SAILS.
posts.caption: Monday morning the wringer washer came rumbling to life in the basement, and by nine o'clock the clothesline was full. Mom had a mouth full of wooden clothespins and a system nobody else understood. Sheets on the outside line, towels in the middle, unmentionables hidden in the back where the neighbors couldn't see. If a cloud rolled in, the whole house ran out back like the building was on fire. And the kids weren't allowed to run between the sheets, which is exactly why we did it every single week. Those sheets came in smelling like sunshine, and nothing out of a box has ever smelled that good since.
posts.first:
My grandmother would check the sky every Monday morning like a ship captain before she hung a single sock. She kept her clothespins in an apron with one big pocket across the front. I can still hear that line squeak on the pulley.

posts.quote: A DOLLAR A CARLOAD, A SPEAKER ON THE WINDOW, AND KIDS IN PAJAMAS IN THE BACK SEAT.
posts.caption: Friday night meant piling in the car with the kids already in their pajamas and a grocery sack of popcorn from home. Dad would back into the spot so we could see over the hood, then reach out and hook that heavy metal speaker on the window. It crackled more than it talked. The cartoon came on, then the first feature, and somewhere in the middle of the second one, every kid in the back seat was asleep in a pile. Dad always forgot the speaker was still on the window. Every drive-in in America had a few dangling cords from somebody who drove off with one.
posts.first:
We went to the drive-in out on the county road every summer, and Mom brought a thermos of lemonade and a stack of napkins. I made it to the second movie exactly once. I woke up in my own bed and couldn't figure out how I got there.

posts.character: Humor about today vs. then (the party line)
posts.quote: THE PARTY LINE / ONE TELEPHONE LINE, FOUR FAMILIES, AND ALWAYS SOMEBODY LISTENING IN
posts.caption: You picked up the phone to call your best friend, and somebody was already on it. Mrs. Pruitt from two houses down, talking about her gallbladder. You hung up gently, waited a minute, and picked it up again, and she was still going. Everybody had their own ring, two longs and a short or whatever it was, and you learned to tell yours from across the house. You also learned that anything you said on that line would be all over the church by Sunday. We didn't call it privacy. We called it being careful.
posts.first:
Our ring was one long and two shorts, and my mother could hear it from the backyard with the radio on. There was a lady on our line who picked up every single time, and you could hear her clock ticking in the background. Nobody ever said a word about it. We all just knew.
